title: Structure–Transport Coupling Under Temperature and Finite-Size Effects in Lennard–Jones Liquids Using Molecular Dynamics Simulations
content: Understanding how microscopic liquid structure governs macroscopic transport remains a fundamental challenge in statistical mechanics. Although the Lennard–Jones (LJ) fluid is a benchmark model for liquid-state studies, the combined effects of temperature and finite system size on structure and transport have rarely been investigated within a unified framework. Here, equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations were performed to examine a three-dimensional LJ liquid over a broad range of temperatures and system sizes. Structural evolution was characterized using the radial distribution function (RDF) and coordination number, while molecular transport was analyzed through the mean-square displacement, velocity autocorrelation function, and self-diffusion coefficients obtained independently from the Einstein and Green–Kubo formalisms. Finite-size effects were corrected using the Yeh–Hummer approach to obtain thermodynamic-limit diffusion coefficients. Increasing temperature reduced the coordination number from 11.8 to 9.1, shortened the cage relaxation time from 18 to 4, and increased the self-diffusion coefficient more than sixfold, from at to at . Diffusion coefficients from the Einstein and Green–Kubo methods agreed within 5%, while finite-size effects caused underestimation of diffusion by up to 28% in the smallest systems. Quantitative scaling relationships linking diffusion with RDF peak height, coordination number, cage relaxation time, and momentum correlation demonstrate that diffusion is governed by the coupled evolution of microscopic structure and dynamical relaxation rather than thermal energy alone.
